---
title: "From Bi-allelic to Multi-allelic Markers"
editor:
  markdown:
    wrap: 72

## From two versions to many

We know that genomic selection reads genetic markers to predict traits.
The most common marker is the SNP. A SNP is a single position in the
genome where only two versions are possible. At that spot, some
individuals carry an A allele, and the rest carry a G allele. Because
there are only two allele versions, we call a SNP bi-allelic.

This is simple, but simple comes at a price. With only two versions, we
can sort individuals into just two groups. That is a very rough way to
tell them apart. A single letter carries very little information on its
own.

Remember that a marker only works because it sits close to a QTL, so the
two are usually passed down together. But this pairing can break. When a
parent passes DNA to its offspring, the chromosome is cut and rejoined
in new places. Each time this happens, a marker and its QTL can end up
separated. Once they are apart, the marker no longer points to anything.
A single SNP is easy to separate in this way.

## Reading words instead of letters

The idea here is simple. Instead of reading one position at a time, we
read a few nearby positions together.

Consider a short piece of DNA, only about 125 letters long, that
contains a few SNPs. Instead of treating each SNP on its own, we read
all of them as one unit. This small combined marker is called a
microhaplotype.

![A microhaplotype consists of several SNPs within a short DNA
segment.](../assets/microhaplotype.png){fig-alt="Microhaplotype built from several SNPs"}

Now look at what happens to the number of versions. A single SNP has
only two. But a short piece of DNA with several SNPs can be written in
many different ways. Where a SNP gives us two options, a microhaplotype
gives us many. Because it can take many values instead of two, we call
it multi-allelic.

Think of it as the difference between a single letter and a short word.
The letter "A" is just one letter. But a three-letter word can be one of
thousands. The word holds far more information.

## When two individuals share the same version

Here is something worth noticing. When two individuals carry the same
version of a marker, there are two possible reasons.

The first reason is coincidence. They happen to carry the same letter,
but they got it from different places, with no shared history.
Geneticists call this a match by state, or identity-by-state.

The second reason is shared inheritance. Both individuals inherited the
very same piece of DNA from a common ancestor. Geneticists call this a
match by descent, or identity-by-descent.

The difference matters a lot. A coincidental match tells us almost
nothing. But a match by descent is powerful. If two individuals
inherited the same stretch of DNA from an ancestor, they very likely
inherited the same nearby QTL along with it. That is exactly the link we
are after.

Now compare the two kinds of marker. A single SNP has only two versions,
so sharing one is cheap. Huge numbers of unrelated individuals carry the
same letter purely by chance, so most matches are just coincidence.

A microhaplotype is different. Because it can take many versions, two
individuals sharing the exact same long word by chance is far less
likely. So when they do share it, they probably share it because they
inherited it from the same ancestor. In short, a multi-allelic marker
turns more matches into the meaningful kind.

## Why more versions help

More versions means each marker tells us more.

Go back to the signpost from the last section. A bi-allelic marker is
like a signpost that can only point left or right. A multi-allelic
marker is like a signpost that can show many different messages. It
tells us where the QTL is much more precisely.

It also stays linked to its QTL more reliably. Because it reads more of
the DNA around the QTL, it is harder to separate the two when a
chromosome is cut and rejoined. And it is better at tracking rare
versions of a trait. A single letter often misses these, but a longer
word can still catch them.

There is a bonus too. Because each microhaplotype carries so much
information, we need fewer markers to get the same picture, or an even
better one. Fewer markers, but each one doing more work.

## What this means in practice

The best part of this approach is that it asks for almost nothing new.

Microhaplotypes are built from SNPs we already have. If a piece of DNA
has already been sequenced, its SNPs are already there. We just choose
to read them together instead of one by one. So the extra information
costs nothing more. There is no new machine to buy and no new sample to
collect.

It is worth being honest about the limits. Microhaplotypes are not a
magic fix. Their advantage is clearest with certain prediction methods
and certain traits, and smaller in other cases. But the main lesson
holds. Moving from two versions to many gives us markers that carry more
information, stay linked to the traits we care about, and cost nothing
extra to build.
